questions.prompt: What is the chapter trying to do with inconsistency?
choices: Treat it as a pattern to analyze rather than only a surprise to notice
Prove that one mismatch explains the whole system
Replace judgment with rules immediately

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter widens from isolated surprises to structured pattern analysis.
explanation.direct: Correct. The move is from one inconsistency toward analysis of repeated variation.
explanation.competitive: That is the point. Stop staring at the flare and map the field.

questions.prompt: Why is one inconsistency not enough by itself?
choices: Because one mismatch may still be anecdotal rather than patterned
Because one inconsistency is always a recording error
Because only technical audits can notice variation

explanation.gentle: Exactly. One surprise can matter without fully explaining the structure of variation.
explanation.direct: The chapter says one mismatch may be real and still too isolated to count as full pattern evidence.
explanation.competitive: One flare is too weak to call the map.

questions.prompt: What does analysis ask once visible misses exist?
choices: What kind of variation is happening and what repeated differences reveal
Whether every mismatch should be ignored until a remedy is ready
How to turn one case into a complete theory immediately

explanation.gentle: Right. Analysis works by grouping and comparing repeated differences.
explanation.direct: The chapter asks what sort of unevenness is appearing and whether it forms a real pattern.
explanation.competitive: Analysis wants the shape of the spread, not one dramatic anecdote.

questions.prompt: Jonah has several forecast reads in adjacent cells instead of one odd estimate. What chapter move fits best?
choices: Treat the repeated variation as a pattern question rather than one isolated complaint
Assume the forecasts cancel each other out automatically
Ignore the spread until later remedy chapters

explanation.gentle: Good. The repeated differences give analysis something stronger than one surprise to work with.
explanation.direct: The right move is to ask what kind of variation is showing up across the set rather than arguing over one odd number.
explanation.competitive: He finally has enough spread on the board to stop guessing at the map.

questions.prompt: Priya compares several similar admissions files and sees different standards recurring. What principle does that illustrate?
choices: One dramatic case is enough to explain the whole process
Repeated visible misses can be grouped into a pattern worth analyzing
Standards do not matter once variation appears

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter wants repeated differences lined up so the pattern becomes clearer.
explanation.direct: Grouping visible misses turns isolated mismatch into a more structured problem of variation.
explanation.competitive: Once the repeats line up, the fog starts breaking.

questions.prompt: Why does analysis have to come before remedies here?
choices: Because a blurry problem invites weak fixes
Because remedies are never useful in judgment
Because one inconsistency already tells us enough

explanation.gentle: Correct. The chapter says improvement needs a problem with shape, not just a mood of unevenness.
explanation.direct: Later judgment improvement work depends on knowing the structure of the variation it is trying to answer.
explanation.competitive: Bad fixes grow fast when the map is still blurry.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between complaint and analysis in this chapter?
choices: Complaint notices unevenness; analysis asks what kind of repeated variation is present
Complaint is emotional while analysis is always mathematical
Complaint is wrong whenever analysis is possible

explanation.gentle: Exactly. Analysis gives unevenness structure instead of leaving it as one reaction.
explanation.direct: The chapter moves from saying the judgments feel uneven to asking what pattern of unevenness is actually emerging.
explanation.competitive: Complaint sees the flare. Analysis draws the map.

questions.prompt: Dana asks whether one striking mismatch is really enough to support a full theory. What chapter skill is she using?
choices: Testing whether the evidence has moved beyond anecdote into pattern
Rejecting analysis because no theory can ever be justified
Assuming patterns exist whenever a case is vivid

explanation.gentle: That fits the chapter well. She is making the flare earn the map.
explanation.direct: The move is to distinguish one vivid event from repeated variation strong enough to support pattern analysis.
explanation.competitive: She is forcing the flare to prove it has company.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter resist building a grand theory from one surprise?
choices: Because pattern thinking still has to stay disciplined about what the evidence supports
Because one surprise is never meaningful at all
Because analysis should avoid structure whenever possible

explanation.gentle: Right. The chapter widens beyond anecdote without letting one event carry too much weight.
explanation.direct: Analysis needs recurrence and grouped evidence, not just intensity, if it is going to deserve broader conclusions.
explanation.competitive: The map has to be earned, not announced.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest bridge from this chapter into the next one?
choices: Once noise has a clearer shape, judgments can be improved more intelligently
The next chapter abandons analysis and returns to one-off anecdotes
The next chapter proves analysis matters more than judgment

explanation.gentle: Yes. The next move is improvement, but now the problem has enough structure to answer seriously.
explanation.direct: The bridge works because later remedies need a clearer map of the variation they are trying to reduce.
explanation.competitive: Once the map exists, the repair can stop guessing.
